\section{Introduction}

Document-level relation extraction (DocRE) requires identifying semantic relations between entity pairs across multiple sentences, a task where encoder-based methods such as \citet{zhou2021atlop} long dominated.
Recent LLM-based approaches have closed this gap: \citet{autore2024} fine-tune LLMs with structured decomposition for end-to-end extraction, \citet{xu2024lmrc} frame it as multi-choice reading comprehension, and \citet{chen2025docksrag} combine retrieval-augmented generation with structured knowledge.
These methods approach or surpass encoder baselines on DocRED \citep{yao2019docred} and Re-DocRED \citep{tan2022redocred} in extraction accuracy.
Yet every one of them outputs bare relation triplets $(e_h, r, e_t)$ without any indication of \emph{which sentences} in the document support each prediction.
In deployment contexts where predictions feed into clinical knowledge bases, legal due-diligence pipelines, or financial compliance systems, end users cannot verify a prediction without manually locating its textual basis across a multi-page document.

The absence of verifiable evidence creates a practical bottleneck.
Relation extraction outputs are consumed downstream by knowledge graph construction and human decision workflows.
When a system predicts that a drug interacts with a gene, or that a contract clause implies a liability, practitioners must trace each prediction back to source text before acting on it.
Without machine-generated evidence, this verification requires exhaustive manual review of the input document for every predicted relation.
Encoder-based methods have partially addressed this need: \citet{xiao2022sais} introduce sentence-level evidence supervision as an auxiliary signal, and \citet{ma2023dreeam} extend this with dynamic evidence retrieval through memory attention.
Both improve extraction quality \emph{and} produce evidence annotations.
However, encoder methods now trail LLM-based approaches in extraction accuracy, and their evidence mechanisms (binary sentence classification) do not transfer to generative architectures.
The community therefore faces a gap: the most accurate extractors provide no evidence, while the evidence-capable methods are no longer competitive.

This gap reflects a deeper structural difference between evidence in encoder and generative frameworks.
In SAIS and DREEAM, evidence retrieval is a binary classification task (does sentence $s_i$ support relation $r$?) that serves as auxiliary supervision.
The evidence signal \emph{regularizes} the encoder and improves extraction.
In LLM-based DocRE, evidence-grounded extraction requires the model to \emph{generate} complete evidence sentences as part of its output sequence, substantially increasing output length and decoding complexity.
Evidence production in this setting is not an auxiliary signal but an additional generation burden that competes with the extraction objective for model capacity.
Whether this generation cost necessarily harms extraction, or whether the interaction is more nuanced, remains an open question: the answer may depend on model scale and optimization strategy.
This uncertainty motivates a systematic investigation of how evidence production interacts with extraction quality across model scales and optimization paradigms.

We formalize evidence-grounded DocRE as a structured generation task for LLMs and conduct a systematic comparison of three post-training optimization paradigms: online reinforcement learning via Group Relative Policy Optimization (GRPO; \citealt{shao2024deepseekmath}), offline preference optimization via Direct Preference Optimization (DPO; \citealt{rafailov2023direct}), and offline reinforcement learning via Rejection Sampling Fine-Tuning (RSFT, building on STaR; \citealt{zelikman2022star}).
Our experiments across 85+ configurations, spanning four model scales (1.7B to 8B), two model families, and two datasets, reveal three principal findings.
\textbf{First}, we identify a \emph{decoupling spectrum}: the strength of RL optimization pressure correlates with the severity of evidence-extraction decoupling.
GRPO with Quantized Low-Rank Adaptation (QLoRA; \citealt{hu2022lora}) produces catastrophic decoupling where extraction accuracy collapses to near zero; GRPO with full-precision training shows mild decoupling; DPO exhibits gradual degradation; and RSFT maintains stable joint performance.
Catastrophic extraction collapse co-occurs with QLoRA-based GRPO training, though we note that GRPO with full-precision training (bf16, $G{=}8$) achieves EDCR below the SFT baseline, indicating that the decoupling is not inherent to online RL when sufficient precision is available.
\textbf{Second}, we discover a \emph{scale-dependent evidence tax}: the cost of jointly producing evidence and relations varies across model scales.
At 1.7B parameters, evidence generation provides an implicit regularization benefit of +6.2pp Ign-F1 on a controlled evaluation subset; at 4B, it imposes a $-$7.5pp penalty; at 8B, the tax approaches zero.
This pattern challenges the assumption that evidence generation uniformly harms extraction.
\textbf{Third}, RSFT with NLI-based scoring for training data selection emerges as the most effective optimization route.
By selecting high-quality training samples through output filtering rather than applying gradient-based optimization pressure, RSFT sidesteps the multi-objective competition that destabilizes RL and preference methods.

Our contributions are as follows:
\begin{enumerate}
    \item We formalize \textbf{evidence-grounded document-level relation extraction} as a generation task for LLMs and conduct the first \textbf{comprehensive empirical study} spanning 85+ experiments across four model scales, two model families, two datasets (DocRED, Re-DocRED), and three optimization paradigms.

    \item We characterize a \textbf{decoupling spectrum} across optimization paradigms: RL optimization pressure is associated with evidence-extraction decoupling severity (GRPO catastrophic $\rightarrow$ DPO gradual $\rightarrow$ RSFT none). We use the Evidence-Decoupling Ratio (EDCR), a diagnostic that tracks misalignment between extraction and evidence capabilities, as an analytical tool throughout our study. EDCR shares Rel-Recall with Rel-F1 by construction; we interpret the observed cross-method correlation ($\rho = -0.89$, $n = 7$) as a diagnostic pattern rather than an independent finding, and validate through per-relation analysis ($\rho = -0.79$, $n = 76$) that avoids the shared-component concern.

    \item We identify a \textbf{scale-dependent evidence tax}: the cost of joint evidence production varies across 1.7B, 4B, and 8B parameters, challenging the assumption that evidence generation uniformly degrades extraction quality.

    \item We establish \textbf{RSFT with NLI-based scoring} as an effective solution, using CED or flat-NLI to select high-quality training data. RSFT achieves +4.92pp Ign-F1 over SFT at 4B scale (four-seed mean), and our 1.7B RSFT model (51.22 Ign-F1) surpasses 8B SFT performance (50.51), enabling deployment-efficient evidence-grounded extraction at reduced computational cost.
\end{enumerate}

\begin{abstract}

Large Language Model (LLM) based Document-level Relation Extraction (DocRE) methods now match or exceed encoder baselines in extraction accuracy, yet they produce bare relation triplets without identifying the sentences that support each prediction.
In deployment contexts such as clinical knowledge bases and legal due-diligence systems, users cannot verify predictions without manually locating textual evidence across multi-page documents.
Encoder-based evidence methods (SAIS, DREEAM) can produce supporting sentences but trail LLM approaches in accuracy. The community therefore faces a gap between extractive precision and output verifiability.

We formalize evidence-grounded DocRE as a structured generation task and conduct a systematic comparison of three post-training optimization paradigms: Group Relative Policy Optimization (GRPO), Direct Preference Optimization (DPO), and Rejection Sampling Fine-Tuning (RSFT).
Our study spans 85+ experimental configurations across four model scales (1.7B to 8B parameters), two model families, and two datasets.
We use the Evidence-Decoupling Ratio (EDCR) as a diagnostic tool and NLI-based scoring for sample selection.

Three findings emerge.
First, RL optimization pressure correlates with evidence-extraction decoupling severity: GRPO causes catastrophic decoupling, DPO shows gradual degradation, and RSFT preserves stable joint performance.
Second, the cost of evidence production varies across model scales: at 1.7B parameters evidence provides a +6.2pp Ign-F1 benefit on a controlled evaluation subset excluding truncated and repetitive outputs, at 4B it imposes a $-$7.5pp penalty, and at 8B the cost approaches zero.
Third, RSFT with NLI-based scoring is the most effective route: it achieves +4.92pp Ign-F1 over supervised fine-tuning at 4B scale (four-seed mean), and our 1.7B RSFT model (51.22 Ign-F1) surpasses 8B SFT performance (50.51).

\end{abstract}

RSFT operates differently: it selects complete outputs and trains on them with standard supervised loss. Because the selection is discrete (accept or reject a full response), there is no gradient pathway through which the model can learn to sacrifice extraction for evidence quality. Only outputs where both extraction and evidence are jointly strong survive the CED filter. This property is not specific to RSFT's design but is a structural consequence of discrete selection over complete outputs: any selection-based method that filters on a joint quality criterion will inherit the same coupling guarantee. The implication for practitioners is direct: when optimizing for multiple coupled generation objectives, selection-based methods preserve inter-objective balance that gradient-based methods disrupt.

164	On Re-DocRED~\citep{tan2022redocred}, the SFT baseline achieves 36.59 Ign-F1 (Evi-F1 81.70, EDCR 0.6674). RSFT CED improves this to 41.45 Ign-F1 (Evi-F1 81.82, EDCR 0.6210), a +4.86pp gain that closely matches the +4.92pp improvement on DocRED. This consistency across datasets with different annotation protocols confirms that RSFT's benefit generalizes beyond training-set-specific artifacts. Evidence quality remains stable across datasets (Evi-F1 81.82 vs.\ 81.15 on DocRED), and the EDCR reduction ($-0.046$) mirrors the DocRED pattern, further supporting the robustness of CED-based selection.
165	
166	\paragraph{Comparison to supervised methods.}
167	Table~\ref{tab:encoder_comparison} directly compares encoder-based methods with our LLM-based approach. Encoder methods achieve substantially higher extraction performance (Rel-F1 63--65 vs.\ our 45--56), reflecting decades of architecture-specific optimization for the classification formulation. However, their evidence identification operates as binary sentence classification, producing Evi-F1 of 52--56 under a joint evaluation protocol. Our TP-only Evi-F1 exceeds 80\%, indicating that when the model correctly identifies a triple, it produces higher-quality evidence than encoder methods. The joint Evi-F1 gap (36.1 vs.\ 54.15) is driven primarily by extraction performance rather than evidence quality: false-positive and false-negative triples dilute the denominator. Closing this gap requires improving extraction capability of LLM-based methods, an orthogonal direction to the evidence faithfulness problem we address.

(c)~Evidence-Decoupling Ratio (EDCR) reveals near-total decoupling in G=4 QLoRA (extraction collapses to Rel-F1 1.4), while G=8 bf16 maintains healthy ratios.}

203	\section{Error Analysis: SFT vs.\ RSFT}
204	\label{sec:error_analysis}
205	
206	Table~\ref{tab:error_analysis} decomposes the extraction improvements from RSFT into error categories across three scales. Three mechanisms drive the gains consistently:
207	
208	\paragraph{Truncation false negatives.} SFT models frequently hit the generation length limit, producing incomplete outputs that miss triples. RSFT training on compact, high-quality outputs reduces this truncation rate. The effect is strongest at 1.7B ($-841$ truncation FN, $-22$\%), where the SFT model's output length is least controlled.
209	
210	\paragraph{Hallucinated false positives.} CED-based filtering removes training examples with unfaithful predictions, reducing the rate of hallucinated triples at inference. LLaMA benefits most ($-593$ hallucinated FP, $-11.8$\%), suggesting cross-architecture variation in hallucination susceptibility.
211	
212	\paragraph{Duplicate predictions.} RSFT training data, selected for quality, contains fewer repetitive patterns. This propagates to inference, reducing duplicate triples by $11$--$20$\% across scales, with 1.7B showing the largest reduction ($-20.2$\%).
213	
214	\paragraph{Evidence quality unchanged.} Despite substantial extraction improvements, evidence exact-match F1 changes by less than 0.4pp at every scale. RSFT selects for joint extraction-evidence quality, but the evidence signal in CED scoring does not translate into measurable evidence improvement. This suggests that evidence grounding requires targeted optimization (e.g., evidence-specific rewards in RL) rather than data selection alone.
215	
216	\paragraph{Residual difficulty.} The proportion of ``other'' false negatives (triples missed for reasons beyond truncation or formatting) increases by 13--15\% in relative terms after RSFT. As easy errors (truncation, duplication) are eliminated, the remaining error distribution shifts toward harder cases: cross-sentence reasoning, implicit relations, and long-tail entity pairs. The relation types with the largest RSFT gains (participant, conflict, league, screenwriter, operator, contains\_administrative\_territory) involve cross-sentence reasoning or long-tail entities, consistent with RSFT's selection pressure toward diverse, high-quality outputs.

240	\label{sec:edcr_per_relation}
241	
242	Computing EDCR for each of the 76 relation types with $\geq$5 evaluation samples (from the RSFT CED s42 model) reveals that per-relation EDCR correlates strongly with per-relation Rel-F1 ($\rho = -0.79$, $n = 76$, $p < 0.0001$), confirming its utility as a difficulty indicator. Filtering to types with $\geq$5 predictions strengthens the correlation ($\rho = -0.85$, $n = 74$, $p < 0.0001$). Per-relation EDCR is statistically independent of Evi-F1 ($\rho = -0.06$, $p = 0.58$), and Evi-F1 itself shows no association with Rel-F1 ($\rho = -0.01$, $p = 0.91$). These null correlations establish that evidence quality and extraction ability are fully decoupled across relation types. Extreme cases illustrate the diagnostic power: \texttt{date\_of\_birth} has EDCR $= 0.118$ (highly faithful, with extraction and evidence tightly coupled), while \texttt{head\_of\_government} reaches $0.956$ (highly decoupled). This per-relation analysis avoids the shared-component concern present in cross-method EDCR-vs-Rel-F1 correlation, providing independent validation of EDCR's diagnostic utility.

Red bars indicate EDCR $\geq$ 0.70 (severe decoupling), green bars indicate EDCR $<$ 0.30 (healthy evidence grounding). Seven types exhibit EDCR = 1.0.}

252	\section{Qualitative Analysis}
253	\label{sec:qualitative}
254	
255	We present representative examples illustrating three phenomena: evidence quality differences between SFT and RSFT, GRPO format gaming under catastrophic collapse, and per-relation EDCR diagnostics.
256	
257	\paragraph{Case 1: Evidence quality.}
258	Table~\ref{tab:case_evidence} compares evidence citations from SFT and RSFT on three documents. SFT tends to cite many sentences indiscriminately, including distractors unrelated to the target triple, while RSFT selects precisely the gold evidence sentences. For \emph{America's Sweetheart}, SFT cites 6 sentences (precision 0.17) whereas RSFT cites only the single correct sentence (precision 1.00). The pattern is consistent: SFT achieves evidence precision of 0.00--0.20 across these examples, while RSFT achieves 1.00 in all three cases.
259	
260	\begin{table}[t]
261	\centering
262	\caption{Evidence citation comparison between SFT and RSFT. Precision measures the fraction of cited sentences that match gold evidence.}
263	\label{tab:case_evidence}

266	\begin{tabular}{llccc}

268	\textbf{Document} & \textbf{Triple} & \textbf{SFT Prec.} & \textbf{RSFT Prec.} & \textbf{SFT \#Cited} \\
269	\midrule
270	Oleg Tinkov & (Oleg Tinkov, country of citizenship, Russia) & 0.00 & 1.00 & 3 \\
271	America's Sweetheart & (record label, country, United States) & 0.17 & 1.00 & 6 \\
272	Jade (Mortal Kombat) & (Jade, present in work, Mortal Kombat) & 0.20 & 1.00 & 5 \\
273	\bottomrule
274	\end{tabular}%
275	}
276	\end{table}
277	
278	\paragraph{Case 2: GRPO format gaming.}
279	Under catastrophic collapse (GRPO QLoRA $G{=}4$), the model abandons the DocRED 96-type relation ontology and generates free-text relation labels. On the document \emph{Something to Believe In}, the model produces 35 predicted triples with relations such as ``is a'', ``honor'', and ``location'', none of which belong to the target ontology. All 35 predictions are incorrect. Similarly, for \emph{J\'{o}zef Pi\l{}sudski Monument}, 28 predictions use non-standard relations with 0 correct matches. The model retains the structural format of triple-with-evidence output but fills it with fabricated relation types. The model produces well-formed evidence for these non-existent relations.
280	
281	\paragraph{Case 3: EDCR diagnostics.}
282	Per-relation EDCR identifies specific relation types where extraction and evidence are misaligned. For \texttt{date\_of\_birth} (EDCR $= 0.118$), the model's evidence consistently matches gold annotations: both extraction and evidence point to the same biographical sentence. In contrast, \texttt{notable\_work} (EDCR $= 0.941$) exhibits severe decoupling: the model cites sentence [0] (a general introduction) instead of the gold evidence sentence [3] (which contains the actual work attribution). High-EDCR relations tend to involve indirect or multi-hop reasoning where surface-level context misleads the evidence generator.
